questions.q: Manus says to leave failures in the context. Doesn't collapsing them contradict that?
questions.a: Manus's point is that a failed action with its error steers the model away from repeating it. The same post warns that a context full of similar action-and-result pairs makes the model follow the pattern. Keep one failure and its error as a note; drop the copies (our reconciliation of the two). Manus's own fix for copycat runs is small variation in wording and format; ours is removing the copies.

questions.q: Won't rewriting the history break the prompt cache?
questions.a: Yes: cached pricing needs the prompt to start with exactly the same text as before (guide 6), so a rewrite makes everything after it full price for one step. Collapse only when the repeat-blocker fires, not every turn, and the cost is small next to eleven wasted calls (our reasoning).

teach.title: How it works: why it repeats, and what the harness does

questions.q: How would you decide when to stop retrying?
questions.a: Count identical calls (same tool, same arguments, same error) in a row; after two, the harness blocks the third and says why. After a few different failures in a row, end the run with a clear error or hand it to a person. The thresholds are our choice; tune them on real traces.

teach.title: How it works: why it repeats, and what the harness does

questions.q: Why doesn't a prompt line telling an agent to note failures and switch approach raise task success?
questions.a: It changes what the model writes, not what it reads: the run of identical failures stays in context, and models continue patterns. Sinha et al. found prompting models to re-check their work gave mixed results, while cutting the history helped one model on their task.

questions.q: What is self-conditioning, in Sinha et al.'s study?
questions.a: Models become more likely to make mistakes when their context holds their own earlier errors. They showed it by planting errors in chat histories on a long running-sum task; larger models were affected too, though Qwen3 with thinking on was not.

teach.title: How it works: why it repeats, and what the harness does

questions.q: Name three harness changes for an agent stuck repeating a failing tool call.
questions.a: Block identical failing calls after a couple of tries; collapse the failed attempts, each call with its result, into one note with the error; and repair, replace or hide the broken tool.
